title: Start with why -- how great leaders inspire action | Simon Sinek | TEDxPugetSound
transcript: Reviewer: Yavor Ivanov What do you start with when you host an event about combining life and passion? You start with the question "why". Why? This sets us up for our first speaker today, Simon Sinek, and his talk, "Start with Why." We take it for granted that we know why we do the things we do. What is the explanation then if they don't turn out as we think. Or what is the explanation when others manage to achieve something that contradicts all assumptions? For example, why is Apple so innovative? Year after year they are more innovative than their competitors. After all, they are just a computer company. They are just like everyone else. They have equal access to talented people, intermediaries, consultants, and information channels. Why then do they seem to be different? Why did Martin Luther King lead the Civil Rights Movement? He was not the only victim in the US at the time, and he certainly was not the only good speaker. Why him? Why were the Wright brothers able to figure out how to make a human-controlled flight, while there were certainly other teams, more qualified than them, better funded, who were unable to make such a flight? The Wright Brothers beat them to it. There is some other factor here. About three and a half years ago I made a discovery. This discovery profoundly changed my perspective on how the world works and profoundly changed the way I live in it. It turned out there was a pattern. It turns out that all the great and inspiring leaders and organizations around the world, whether it's Apple, Martin Luther King, or the Wright Brothers, they all think, act, and communicate in the same way. And he's the opposite of what everyone else is doing. My contribution is that I formulated it, and it's probably the simplest idea in the world. I call it the "Golden Circle." Why? How? What? This little idea explains why some organizations and leaders are able to inspire and others cannot. Let's go over the concepts very quickly. Absolutely every person, absolutely every organization on the planet knows WHAT they are doing, 100 percent. Some know HOW they do it, whether it's called differentiated user benefit or specialized technology or written procedures. However, there are very few people or organizations who know WHY they do what they do. And by "why" I don't mean "for profit." This is a result. It 's always just a result. By "why" I mean: What is your goal? What is your cause? What do you believe in? Why does your organization exist? Typically, the way we think, act, and communicate is determined by the external environment. It 's obvious. We go from what is clear to what is unclear. But inspiring leaders and organizations, regardless of their size, regardless of their field of activity, all think, act, and communicate from the inside out. Let me give you an example. I use Apple because it's easy to understand and everyone gets it. If Apple were like everyone else, their marketing message would be: "We make great computers. They're beautifully designed, easy to use, and affordable. Do you want to buy one?" "Emmies..." That's exactly how most of us communicate. This is how much of marketing is done, much of sales is done, and most of us communicate with each other this way. We say what we do, how we are different or why we are better, and we expect specific behavior, a purchase, a vote, something like that. This is our new law firm. We have the best lawyers with the biggest clients. We always succeed with the work assigned by our clients. Here's our new car, it has low fuel consumption, leather seats... buy our car. But that doesn't inspire you. This is how Apple actually communicates. "Everything we do challenges the status quo. We believe in thinking differently. Our way of challenging the status quo is by designing our products beautifully and making them easy to use. That's how you make great computers. Do you want one? Big difference, right? You're ready to buy a computer from me. I've just reversed the order of the information. People don't buy what you do, they buy the reason you do it. People don't buy what you do, they buy the reason you do it. That's why every person in this room would be perfectly willing to buy a computer from Apple. We 'd also be perfectly willing to buy an MP3 player from Apple, or an Apple phone, or an Apple DVR. But, as I said before, Apple is just a computer company. There's nothing that structurally sets them apart from any of their competitors. They're equally qualified to make all of these products. In fact, they tried. A few years ago, Gateway created flat-screen TVs. They're extremely qualified to make flat screen TVs. They've been doing this for years. Nobody bought them. Dell made MP3 players and PDAs, they also work great and they can also have great designs on their products - but nobody bought them. Just talking about it now we can't even imagine buying an MP3 player from Dell. Why would anyone buy an MP3 player from a computer company? But we do it every day. People don't buy what you do, they buy the reason you do it. The goal is not to sell to everyone who needs your product. The goal is to sell to those people who have the same beliefs as you. Here's the most important thing: none of what I've said so far is my opinion. It's all based on the principles of biology. Not psychology, biology. If we look at a cross-section of the human brain and look at it from above, we will see that the human brain is divided into three main components that perfectly associate with the golden circle. Our newest brain, The Homo sapiens brain, our neocortex, is responsible for the "WHAT" level. The neocortex is responsible for all of our rational and analytical skills, thought and language. The middle two sections are our limbic brain, and it's responsible for all of our feelings, like trust and loyalty. It's also responsible for our behavior, decision-making, and it has no ability to express itself verbally. In other words, when we communicate from the outside in, people can understand a lot of complex information like features and extras, facts and numbers. But it doesn't trigger behavior. When we can communicate from the inside out, we're talking directly to that part of the brain that controls behavior, and then we're allowing people to rationalize it through the factuality of our words or actions. That explains intuitive decisions. You know, sometimes you can provide all of the facts and indicators, and people say, "I know all of these facts and details, but it just doesn't feel right." Why do we use this verb "feel"? Because that part of the brain that makes decisions doesn't have language. And the best we can mutter is "I don't know. "I don't feel it right," or sometimes it's said that you follow your heart or you follow your soul. I hate to disappoint you, but it's not about the parts of your body that control your behavior. It all happens here, in your limbic brain, the part of your brain that's responsible for decisions, not language. But if you don't know why you do what you do, and people respond to the reason you do it, then how are you ever going to get anyone to vote for you, or buy something from you, or even be loyal and want to be a part of what you do? Again, the goal is not just to sell to people who need your product. The goal is to sell to people who share your beliefs. The goal is not just to hire people who need a job, but to hire people who share your beliefs. I always say that if you hire people just because they can do the job, they're going to do it for the money. But if you hire people who believe in the same things that you do, they're going to work for You with all your dedication. We can't think of a better example of that than the Wright brothers. Most people don't know about Samuel Pierpont Langley. In the early 20th century, achieving human-controlled flight was a big deal. Everyone was trying to achieve it. Samuel Pierpont Langley had what we would consider a recipe for success. Even now, when you ask people, "Why did your product or company fail?" they always answer with some variation of the same three things: insufficient capital, the wrong people, bad market conditions. They always say those three things, so let's explore them. The War Department gave Samuel Pierpont Langley $50,000 to create such a flying machine. Money was no problem. He taught at Harvard and worked for the Smithsonian, he had the best connections. He knew all the great minds of the time. He hired the smartest people, and the market conditions were incredible. The New York Times followed him everywhere. and everyone was rooting for Langley. How come we'd never heard of him then? Hundreds of miles away, in Dayton, Ohio, Orville and Wilbur Wright had none of what we would call a recipe for success. They had no money, they paid for their dream with the proceeds of their bicycle shop, none of their team had a college degree, not even Orville and Wilbur themselves, and the New York Times did n't even know they existed. The difference was that Orville and Wilbur were working for a cause, for a purpose, for a belief. They believed that if they could build a flying machine, it would change the course of the world. Samuel Pierpont Langley was different. He wanted to be rich and he wanted to be famous. He chased results. He chased fortune. And look what happened. The people who believed in the Wright brothers' dream worked with them with complete dedication. The others just worked for a paycheck. Stories are told of how every time the Wright brothers They went out, took 5 sets of parts, and they broke down so many times before they got home. Finally, on December 17, 1903, the Wright brothers flew, and there wasn't even a single witness. Everyone found out about it a few days later. Another piece of evidence that Langley was wrongly motivated: the day the Wright brothers flew, he quit. He could have said, "This is an amazing discovery, guys, I'm going to build on your technology," but he didn't. He wasn't first, he was n't rich, he wasn't famous, so he quit. People don't buy what you do, they buy why you do it. If you talk about what you believe in, you'll attract those who believe in the same thing. And why is it important to attract those who believe in the same thing? It's called the law of diffusion of innovation. If you don't know the law, you've probably heard the term. The top two and a half percent of the population are our innovators. The Next 13 And then there's the early adopters, the next 34 percent, the early majority, and then there's the late majority, the laggards. The latter are buying touchscreen phones because they can't afford flip phones anymore. (Laughter) We 're all at different places on that scale at times, but what the law of diffusion of innovation tells us is that if you want to achieve mass market success or mass adoption of an idea, it's not going to happen until you reach that tipping point, between 15 and 18 percent approval, where the system flips. I like to ask businesses, "How many people are buying your new products?" The proud answer is: "About 10 percent." But that could just be a coincidence. You can always just "get by" with 10%. That's even how we describe them. Like with the feeling. "Oh, they just work." The problem is how to reach those who do if they don't know you yet. Our job is to fill that little gap, as Jeffrey Moore calls it, "to bridge the gap." Because this early majority won't try something until someone else tries it before them. These people here, the innovators and early adopters, have no problem making intuitive decisions. They are more likely to make intuitive decisions that are guided by their beliefs about the world and not simply by the qualities of the product. These are the people who stood in line for 6 hours to buy an iPhone when it first came out. Or they could just go next week and not wait. These are the people who spent $40,000 on a flat screen TV when it first came out, even though the technology was substandard. They didn't do it because the technology is great, but for their own sake. Because they wanted to be first. People don't buy what you do, they buy the reason you do it. What you do is only proof of what you believe. People actually do the things that prove their beliefs. The reason you buy an iPhone in the first 6 hours, standing in line for 6 hours, is related to your beliefs about the world and how you want others to see you: They were first. People don't buy what you do, they buy the reason you do it. Let me give you a famous example, a famous failure and a famous success of the law of diffusion of innovation. First the famous failure. The example is commercial. As we said a moment ago, the recipe for success is money, the right people, and the right market conditions. Right? Then you must be successful. Look at TiVo. From the moment TiVo came out 8-9 years ago until today, they remain the highest quality product on the market, there is no dispute about that. They were very well funded. Market conditions were fantastic. We even use TiVo as a verb. I "tweet" cable shows all the time. But TiVo was a commercial failure. They failed to make any money. When they went public, their shares were $30-40, and then they fell and never rose above $10. I don't even think they trade above $6, except for some brief spikes. When TiVo launched their product, they told us about its features. They said, "We have a product that pauses the TV, skips commercials, skips parts of the show, and remembers your preferences without you even asking." And the cynical majority said, "We don't believe you. We don't need this. We don't like it. You're scaring us." What if they had said: "If you're someone who likes to have complete control over every aspect of your life, then this product is for you. Let me now give you a successful example of the law of diffusion of innovation. In the summer of 1963, 250,000 people came to the park in Washington to hear Dr. King speak. There were no invitations sent out, no website to check the date. How did they do it? Dr. King was not the only great orator in America. He was not the only person suffering from a lack of rights. In fact, some of his ideas were not good. But he had a gift. He didn't go around preaching what needed to change in America. He traveled around and spoke about what he believed in. "I believe, I believe, I believe," he said. And people who believed the same thing adopted his cause as their own and passed it on to others. Some of these people created structures to reach even more people. And look, 250,000 people came on the right day, at the right time, to hear him speak. How many of them went there because of him? Zero. They have gone for themselves. Their beliefs about America led them to travel 8 hours by bus and stand under the sun in Washington in the middle of August. Because of their beliefs, and not just blacks versus whites: 25% of the audience was white. Dr. King believed that there were two types of laws in the world: those made by a higher authority and those made by people. And only when the laws made by people correspond to the laws made by a higher authority will we live in a just world. And so it happened that the Civil Rights Movement became the ideal channel for pursuing his cause. We followed him, not for him, but for ourselves. And by the way, his speech begins with "I have a dream," not "I have a plan." (laughter) Listen to the politicians today with their 12-point plans. They don't inspire anyone. Because there are leaders and there are those who lead. Leaders have a position of power or authority, but those who lead inspire us. Whether they are people or organizations, we follow those who lead, not because we have to, but because we want to. We follow those who lead, not for their sake, but for ourselves.
